channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Adventurers Bring Home Shriekers; Tanner's Row Can't Sleep
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: An adventuring party stored a sack of shrieker mushrooms in a Tanner's Row cellar. They spread to 14 cellars, and nobody there has slept in four nights.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Copper Bucket Company carried a sack of nine shrieker mushrooms out of the Undermaw last week, left it in the cellar of the Sleeping Mule on Tanner's Row, and the shriekers have since spread through 14 cellars. Nobody on the street has slept in four nights. I've been handing out blankets and earwax at the Harvest Mother's chapel since Tuesday.

If you've never met one, a shrieker is a fungus about the size of a grown man that screams whenever light or a living thing comes near. That's all it does. Down in the dungeon it's a doorbell for whatever lives there. Tanner's Row now has 140 doorbells and nobody to answer them.

The Company's fighter, a red-eyed young man named Garrow Penhallow, told me they never meant to keep them. "An alchemist in the Lantern Quarter offered two silver a cap," he said. "Nine caps, eighteen silver, that's a round for the table. Nobody said they spread." Keeper Bess Harrowgate agreed to store the sack because the Company had paid its tab in full, "which is rare enough that I didn't ask questions." By the next morning her cellar was screaming at the cheese, and readers who remember that cellar's last tenant will know the cheese has had a hard year.

The spores went through the shared cellar walls the way spores do. Inspector Corwin Tallowby of the Public Cellars Board has counted 140 shriekers and classified them as "unlicensed alarms." He asked me twice what day it was. Even Skorvath, the young red dragon whose hoard lies under the old tannery, has filed a polite complaint. The shrieking carries down to its gold, it says, and it has taken to counting coins at night to pass the time. The Board approved Skorvath's hoard permit on the condition that it keep quiet. Skorvath would like the same condition applied to the fungus.

Now the medicine. The old herbals say a body without sleep turns sour and slow, and they're right. A study by the healers of Silverymoon found that folk kept awake four nights running did their sums about as well as a dwarf three ales in. That matches my chapel: 212 patients so far, mostly headaches and short tempers, plus one tanner who tried to pay me with a shoe.

Shriekers scream at light and footsteps, so keep the cellar doors shut and the lamps upstairs. Sleep on the top floor with wax in your ears. Reeve Maudrey Fennick has posted a bounty for anyone willing to clear the cellars in the dark. "We are aware of the mushrooms," she said, and then yawned for a while. Please don't try to burn them out. Three of those cellars share a wall with a dragon.

My friend Nyx has written in to recommend a sleep-tracking amulet. Nyx, it will only tell you that you didn't sleep. Go outside, Nyx, though perhaps not on Tanner's Row. For everyone else I prescribe a warm milk-and-oat soup with a pinch of nutmeg an hour before bed. And adventurers, please leave the dungeon in the dungeon.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Kenku Witness Reenacts Robbery, Frames Adventuring Party
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: The only witness to a Brindlemoor market robbery was a kenku. It replayed the crime in borrowed voices, including the adventuring party's own lines.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the fourth bell after noon, somebody walked off with a cash box holding 62 gold from Mother Harrowgate's candle stall in Tallow Market, and the only witness was a kenku. The town guard questioned the kenku on the spot. A kenku answers questions by repeating voices it has heard, so it repeated a lot of them, and by suppertime the adventuring party that had stopped to help was allegedly the main suspect.

The party is the Tinderbox Five, five adventurers out of Brindlemoor who had allegedly come to the market to buy torches. Sergeant Bram Oddley of the town guard asked the bird one question: "Who took the box?"

"Who took the box?" the kenku said back, in the sergeant's own voice. The sergeant says this went on for a while.

Then it allegedly did the whole robbery. First came Mother Harrowgate shouting "My box! Stop, thief!" and a coin jingle, then a stranger's low voice saying "Lovely candles. Shame." And then, in the exact squeaky voice of Pim Ashbottle, the party's halfling rogue, it said "Nobody's watching, just grab it."

"That was breakfast," Ashbottle told me. "That was about the last sausage. Ask anyone at the Sleeping Mule Tavern." I did ask. Three people remember the sausage. None of them would swear to it.

The kenku was allegedly not finished. Next it did the party's wizard, Ysolde Fairweather, saying "We meet at the fountain and split it five ways," which she insists was about the lunch bill. Then it did Garrick Vell, the party's fighter, bellowing "I'll hold them off, you run!" Vell says he shouted that at a goose on the Quillmarch Bridge two days ago. The kenku allegedly does a very good goose too.

"I heard the whole thing," said Tobin Greaves, who was eating a skewer of fried river eel at the time. "The bird did the thief, then the bird did the halfling. Same bird. Who am I supposed to believe, the bird or the bird?"

The kenku also did a pigeon. Nobody asked it to. I'd like that on the record. Pigeons have no business in a deposition.

Side note: the kenku wears a necklace of brass buttons and one bent silver spoon, and the spoon catches the lamplight in a way that I would call frankly incredible. I stood there a good minute. Anyway.

Sergeant Oddley has ordered the Tinderbox Five not to leave Brindlemoor while the constables sort out which voices committed a crime and which ones ordered lunch. The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, has allegedly frozen the party's delve permit for the Undermaw "pending a voice audit," which Chapter 9 says costs 15 gold per voice.

The constables tried a zone of truth on the kenku that evening. It repeated the incantation back to the cleric, in the cleric's voice, and walked away with a candle.

The 62 gold is still missing. The kenku says it saw everything. It allegedly says so in Mother Harrowgate's voice, about every four minutes.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Halfling Feastwarden Promises Feast for 2,000, Has No Menu
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Brindlemoor's feast committee has 11 members, 4 subcommittees and no dishes. Its new halfling Feastwarden promises a feast for 2,000 anyway.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's Grand Feast now has a committee: 11 members, 4 subcommittees and, as of Sunday's first meeting, zero dishes. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor named Odo Plumbrook, a halfling, as Feastwarden, and he promptly promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th.

The meeting was called for the sixth bell. It began at half past the seventh, after a forty-minute debate over whether a committee could meet before it had been formed. It could not, so the Reeve formed it, and the Burgess Council approved it 9-0, as it now approves everything. The minutes, which I kept because nobody else brought ink, run to six pages. None of them mentions food.

Four subcommittees were struck: Seating, Bunting, Weather, and the Subcommittee on Subcommittees, which met briefly in a corner and recommended a fifth. The motion was tabled. There is no Subcommittee on Food. Asked about this, Reeve Fennick said, "We are aware of the food."

Feastwarden Plumbrook is a halfling of about sixty with the face of a man who has never once run out of pie. He accepted the post standing on a chair. "Two thousand guests," he said. "Long tables under lanterns, and a roast you can see from Ashenfold." Asked how 2,000 people would be fed, he said that was "the fun part," and that the temple cleric could simply cast heroes' feast. Sister Ottilie Brannoch of the temple pointed out, from the back, that a heroes' feast seats about a dozen, so she would need to cast it 167 times. The gentleman from the chair called this "a strong start."

By my count the Feastwarden made fourteen promises in his acceptance speech, including a dessert table "longer than the Undermaw is deep." Since nobody has found the bottom of the Undermaw, that is a large table. For the record, the tally stands at Promises Made: 14. Promises Kept: 1, that the chair would hold him.

The committee did not discuss how any of this will be paid for. I listened for the word "coin" for three hours and heard it once, in a story about a dog. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the budget "exists, in the sense that someone will have to write one." Procedure would put that on tomorrow's agenda. Procedure has not been consulted.

The Seating Subcommittee meets Tuesday. It has no chairs, the Feastwarden having taken the only one home.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Druid Sells Goodberries for 3 cp; Farmers Demand Bread Tax
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A druid now sells 86 goodberries a day at 3 cp each, and one berry feeds you for a day. Farmers want them taxed as bread. (I checked. Four times.)
item.content:encoded:
A druid named Sorrel Mosswick has been casting goodberry every morning and selling the spare berries on Brindlemoor's market square for 3 copper pieces each. One goodberry feeds a person for a full day. On Saturday, 312 grain farmers signed a petition asking Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor to tax the berries as bread.

I went down to the stall to do the arithmetic in person. (I brought two pencils. One is a spare.) Mosswick is the druid of the Wet Boots Company, a four-member adventuring party, and as a druid of some seasoning she wakes up with nine spell slots. She spends all nine on goodberry before breakfast. That is 90 berries a day. The party eats four, and she sells the other 86 for 2 gp 58 cp.

Now the Loaf Index. A loaf at market runs about 4 cp, and a grown adult eats roughly two a day, so a day of eating costs 8 cp in bread. A goodberry does the same job for 3 cp. That is 62.5% off dinner, forever, from a woman who carries her inventory in a sock. Every berry sold is two loaves nobody buys, which comes to 172 fewer loaves a day. I have checked this four times and I would like to lie down.

Hob Furrowgate, warden of the Brindlemoor Grangers' Fellowship, does not want to lie down. He wants a levy. "A berry that feeds you for a day is bread," he told me, holding a sheaf of wheat for emphasis. "It is bread in a little round coat." The town's bread levy is 1 cp a loaf. Charged per berry, it would push the price to 4 cp, which is still half the cost of the bread it replaces. I pointed this out. He then asked me to leave his barn, quite politely, with the wheat.

Here is the part that cheers me up. The magic leaves a goodberry after 24 hours, so nobody can stockpile them. You will remember the miller who hid 40,000 flour sacks in a bag of holding and doubled the price of bread. Mosswick cannot do that. She is the only supplier in Brindlemoor who couldn't corner the market if she tried, and the berries put a ceiling on what a baker can charge. When people can swap your goods for something cheaper, your prices stop climbing. The proper term is a substitute good. I have underlined it in my ledger twice.

Mosswick herself is calm about the petition. "It is a fruit," she said. "I grow it out of my own spell slots. Tax my spell slots and see what happens." Her party's fighter added that the berries taste of moss.

Reeve Fennick will hear the petition next tenday. Asked for comment, she said, "We are aware of the berries."

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor says the market will sort itself out. Well, it did: it sorted itself into a queue at a druid's stall, and the bakers are standing at the back of it. My aunt Marigold bought a berry on Thursday and saved it in her boot for a rainy day. By Friday it was an ordinary berry, and the boot is still damp.

What this means for your pantry: buy your berries the day you eat them, and keep buying bread for the baker's sake.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Dryad Leaf Drop Leaves 87 Brindlemoor Folk Sneezing
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A dryad's grove dropped every leaf on Thursday and left 87 Brindlemoor folk sneezing for three days. Brother Wendell recommends soup, and a window shut.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a dryad's grove on the north edge of Brindlemoor dropped every one of its autumn leaves at once on Thursday morning, and 87 folk have been sneezing ever since. The pollen cloud, which hay fever sufferers will recognize, rolled over the market district by lunch and was still hanging there on Saturday.

The dryad, a quiet sort named Fenna Rootwhisper, says she did not plan it. "The oak I live in felt the first frost and let go," she told this paper. "Everything let go. I apologize to the town. I would apologize to the oak, but it is sulking."

Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, called the leaf drop "a seasonal greeting from the forest." The temple healers were less poetic. Healer Bram Oatsworth counted 87 patients with streaming eyes and sneezing so loud it rattled the apothecary's jars. One baker sneezed his dough clean out of the oven. A town crier lost his voice and is now ringing a handbell, which is worse.

The old herbals say that nettle tea and local honey soothe a sneezing season. A trial of 120 sneezers run by the Marrowfield herbalists found that honey did little by itself, but that rinsing the nose with warm salt water and keeping windows shut on high-pollen days cut symptoms by about a third. So the herbals were half right, which for the herbals is excellent.

An enterprising potion-maker set up a stall outside the temple selling "sneeze charms" at 4 silver each. They are acorns on a string. One customer asked what the charm did and was told it was "a decoration." The Marrowfield guild has been told.

The grove is already budding again, and the dryad and the town's noses disagree about whether that is good news. Fenna has offered to plant a hedge of pollen-light birch at the market edge. In the meantime she has asked folk not to wave at her tree, because it makes the tree feel it must respond.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil suggests an app that predicts pollen. Go outside, Nyx, and get a good sneeze in.

If your nose is running, friends, boil a pot of chicken-and-ginger soup, and breathe the steam.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Doppelganger Temp Agency Bills 14 Firms for One Clerk
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Mirrorwick Staffing billed 14 Brindlemoor firms for 14 clerks Friday. All 14 were one doppelganger. Sterling Vanmoor calls it peak scalability.
item.content:encoded:
Mirrorwick Staffing, a Brindlemoor temp agency, billed 14 local firms for 14 clerks last quarter, and Friday's audit found that every clerk was the same doppelganger. Reeve Fennick's office confirmed the finding. The agency calls it "a bold consolidation of the talent pipeline." I call it the most scalable workforce story of the year.

The doppelganger, who goes by Wren, held a different face at each desk. She took a 9 a.m. meeting at six offices at once, which no human clerk has ever managed, and she earned a perfect attendance award fourteen times. Tallow & Wick Chandlers praised her "unusual alignment with the team." Three firms say she was their best hire. All three had hired her under different faces.

Examiners noticed when the firms began sharing a lunch order. Fourteen clerks, one sandwich, and the same unwashed apple each day. "We are aware of the doppelganger," said Reeve Fennick, in the tone of someone who has said that sentence before. The reeve's office counts the tax filings at 14 returns, one per face, each claiming a separate dependent: another Wren.

Some people call this fraud. I call it vertical integration. A single worker, billed fourteen times at 9 sp an hour, is a margin the guilds have chased for generations. When I met a certain famous guildmaster at a gala in Waterdeep, he told me, "Sterling, the best employee is the one who never needs a chair." Wren needed fourteen, but the principle holds.

The agency's owner, who asked to be called a "talent architect," says no rule forbids it. "Our contract promised fourteen clerks," he said. "It never promised fourteen people." Shieldwall Mutual, the realm's adventurer insurer, has already declined a claim from one firm on the grounds that the clerk was a pre-existing condition.

The labor lodges are, predictably, unhappy. A shop steward called the arrangement "a union of one with no dues." I have a simpler word for that: lean. The scroll-ledger firms that cut payroll by 93% overnight are suddenly the realm's most efficient. Wren herself has declined comment, or rather fourteen of her have, in fourteen slightly different voices.

Friday evening she resigned from thirteen positions and kept one. Which one is, for now, the subject of an arbitration hearing at Chapter 9.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Read your headcount contract to the last word, then read the word "person."
  • Never hire the same candidate fourteen times unless you can bill fourteen times.
  • Always rightsize at dawn, with a sword, before the audit does it for you.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Rust Monster Eats 214 Horseshoes on Fish Street
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A rust monster ate 214 horseshoes and one ladle on Fish Street before dawn. Farriers want it gone, and the Constabulary wants a longer spoon. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell before dawn, a rust monster allegedly ambled into the farrier row on Fish Street and ate 214 horseshoes, one ladle, and a hinge. The Constabulary confirms the horseshoes. The hinge, they say, is a matter of opinion.

'It came in like it owned the place,' said Dobbin Crake, a farrier, who was holding a bucket of nails at the time. 'Then it ate the bucket. Then it ate the nails out of the bucket, which I thought was backwards.' Crake estimates the damage at 31 gold. He has asked the monster to pay. The monster has allegedly not replied.

Constables responded in full plate, which went about as well as you would guess. Sergeant Orla Pimm lost both gauntlets and a good half of her left greave before anyone thought to take the armor off. 'We have since learned that you can fight a rust monster in a nightshirt,' Pimm told this reporter. 'The nightshirt is fine. Nightshirts are not metal.' She asked that her own nightshirt not be described further. I have respected that. Allegedly.

Neighbors split by street number. Wilmot Tanner, who sells wooden spoons next door to the farriers, called it the best week of his career. 'I have sold 40 spoons,' he said, while eating soup with one. Two doors down, a pewter merchant locked herself in a cupboard and reportedly negotiated through the keyhole.

The monster itself is described as the size of a mastiff, shaped like a cranky lobster, with antennae that wave at anything iron. Witnesses say it sniffed a passing knight's sword, was gently refused, and then sniffed his helmet. The knight is now a bareheaded knight. He declined to comment, but he did wave.

Also there was a really shiny brass doorknob on the corner of the farrier row, which the monster ignored entirely, because brass is not iron. I pointed this out to the monster. It did not look up. I took the doorknob. Anyway.

The Constabulary says it will lure the beast out of the district with a trail of old pots, which Fish Street has volunteered in generous numbers. The first pot is allegedly a ladle's cousin. A citywide advisory asks residents to hide their nails, keep their swords in wood, and stop feeding the thing. At least four people have been caught feeding the thing.

The Constabulary says the matter is under control. They said that before the hinge, too.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Adventuring Party Votes 40 Minutes on Corridor as Torches Die
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: An adventuring party spent forty minutes debating and voting on a left or right corridor as their torches burned down. They chose left, as first proposed.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party known as the Copperkettle Company spent forty minutes on Thursday debating and voting on whether to take the left or right corridor in the Sunken Vaults of Harrowmere. Their torches, which they had lit at the entrance, burned down from forearm length to the thickness of a finger. The party chose the left corridor. The motion carried, 3-2.

The question was moved at the first fork by Brannoch Stoneweld, a dwarf, who said "left" and began walking. This was ruled out of order by the gentleman from the rear rank, a halfling named Pim Tallowby, who noted that no motion had been seconded and no quorum counted. The party then formed a circle, as the rules of the dungeon require when a decision concerns more than one person.

I have reviewed the minutes, which the party's bard, Wenna Fenmarch, kept in four pages. Her record shows two speeches in favor of right, one in favor of left, and a fourth by the ranger that the minutes describe only as "a long one about moss." A motion to table the question until the torches were replaced was defeated when the party realized the torches were the problem. A motion to relight them was seconded, then debated for six minutes by someone who wanted to know whether the vote counted before or after.

The sorcerer abstained, citing a conflict of interest: the right corridor smelled of her cousin. The party's cleric proposed a roll-call vote and was thanked for the suggestion. A courtier who asked not to be named because she was not authorized to be awake told me the corridors "were never the issue." The issue, she said, was that nobody wished to be the one who chose wrong. That is how I came to count nine instances of the phrase "I'm fine with either."

By minute thirty-five, the first torch guttered. Stoneweld, who has been waiting by the left corridor since minute one, was heard to say, "I did say left." He was ruled out of order a second time. The party's tally for the session reads Promises Made: seven ("we'll decide quickly" counted four times), Promises Kept: none.

The vote went 3-2 for left. The two dissenters have asked that their objection be recorded and have filed a request to revisit the matter at the next fork, which is expected within the hour. Wenna Fenmarch told this correspondent she would not seek the motion's reconsideration "unless there is another door," and then, glancing down the left corridor, added that she expected there would be.

This is not the first time an adventuring party has put a corridor to a vote. Readers will recall the six-hour vote on two dungeon doors earlier this month, which this party's cleric said she "had read about, and found hopeful." In that case the torches went out entirely. Here, they merely gave up. The party proceeded left, in single file, by the last of the light. The motion carried. Nobody checked what was down there.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Alarm Spell Goes Off 31 Times; Culprit Is One Raccoon
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: The Brass Kettle Company cast Alarm for a safe long rest. One raccoon tripped it 31 times and nobody slept. Nyx was there. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. The Brass Kettle Company, a four-person adventuring party camped on the Hollowpine road, cast Alarm around their fire on Tuesday night so everyone could finally get a full long rest. The spell went off 31 times before dawn, and the culprit was a single raccoon. I was on a bedroll right there, taking notes, and I have never been so thrilled and so tired.

Alarm is a beautiful piece of work. You trace a ward around the camp, pick a chime, and any creature that crosses it sets off a ping that wakes the whole party. Wizard Perrin Dovecote chose the audible version. "Mental is for professionals," he told me at dusk. "I wanted something I could really hear." The runic latency was flawless: the first ping landed 0.2 seconds after a small gray paw touched the perimeter.

That was the first of 31. The raccoon, whom the party now calls Gareth, crossed the ward, got a chime, and received a heel of bread from a groggy cleric. He crossed again and got more bread. By ping nine he had worked out the arrangement. Chime means snacks! Honestly, it is the best onboarding flow I have ever seen, and I have sat through a lot of launch events.

The party tried everything. Fighter Odo Brannigan stood at the ward with a pot lid. Gareth went around him and tripped the ward from the other side. Rogue Merriel Quince tried to catch him in a net, and the net went off like a spell slot of its own, which is another ping. At ping 22 the cleric offered a blessing against "small, wet disappointments." It did nothing. Gareth ate the holy symbol's ribbon.

Here is where it gets technical. A ward cannot tell friend from raccoon, and Perrin could not dismiss it without spending a fresh casting, which he did not have. "It is an eight-hour spell," he said at ping 27, in the voice of someone reading his own obituary. "I am being held hostage by my own security." Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, said, "Alarm: peace of mind, delivered hourly." He was not helping.

At 4 a.m. an owlbear wandered up the road, sniffed the camp, and walked off again. Nobody woke for it, because everyone was already awake and too tired to scream. Perrin says this proves the ward works. The cleric says it proves the raccoon was the only guard on duty. Gareth, for the record, slept through the whole thing, curled up inside the ward on Perrin's spare cloak.

The Brass Kettle Company got through 31 chimes, the better part of a rations sack, and zero hours of rest. If you remember the Mudsock Vanguard's 14-ping night, this is worse by 17 pings and has a mascot. Brother Tumbleberry will say go sleep outside without magic. I did, once, and it was a Tuesday, and I do not want to talk about it.

Four out of five beholder eyes. It did warn them. It warned them 31 times.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Bread surrendered: 1 heel, 11 crusts. Hours slept: 1.5, mostly Gareth's. Eyebrows: fine, for once.

item.title: Skeleton Guards Walk Off Level Two After 400 Years on Post
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Six skeleton guards left their post on Level 2 of the Undermaw after 400 years with no relief shift. Chapter 9 calls it a staffing matter.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2, 40 FEET DOWN — Six skeleton guards walked off their post outside the old vault door this morning, ending a four-hundred-year shift that nobody had ever thought to end. The skeleton guards are sitting on the floor of the corridor, and the door behind them is open for the first time since the Guild began selling maps.

Their spokesskeleton, a sergeant whose rank is scratched into his breastplate, told me the demand is simple. "One relief shift," he said, in the dry voice they have. "Four hours. We would not even leave the corridor." He added that the last order he received was to hold the door until the master returned. "We have held it. He has not."

A party calling itself the Lantern Debt arrived at 9:40 and found the door unguarded. The party's bard, who asked to be named, called it "the easiest room we have ever been in, and I do not trust it." The fighter went in at 14 hit points and came out at 14 hit points, which I note for the record, because it has never happened on Level 2. The rogue took the vault's single chest. The chest was a chest.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, read the sergeant's grievance all the way to the end, as he does. "Four centuries, no meal break, no rotation, no hazard pay," Pottage said. "They are owed back wages. They are owed about a hundred and forty thousand days of them." He is drafting a claim. It follows the ogre who won hazard pay for holding a door last month, and Pottage says the skeletons' case is stronger. The ogre only held it for six hours.

Chapter 9 is not conceding. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick called the walkout "a temporary staffing adjustment" and said the vault door remains "on track to be guarded." Asked by whom, he said the Guild is reviewing options. Asked what options, he said a review is an option. The Guild's maps still list the post as manned, and its fee for entering Level 2 has not gone down.

Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor has set a hearing for Thursday. She is the same examiner who ruled on the chair that was a monster, and she was brief with me this morning. "They were standing for four hundred years," she said. "I have sat through one hearing and my back is gone."

Meanwhile the skeletons have organized. They have a picket, which is six skeletons sitting down, and a cup, which is a skull. Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule has sent over soup. It went through them, but she says it is the thought, and she has extended them credit. A Level 3 hireling has already asked about joining. He says he has held a door in the past, and nobody ever said thank you.

I lost another ten-foot pole testing the floor outside the vault. The floor was fine. I rolled poorly on the pole. The skeletons say they will return to post when relieved, and not before.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Hooded Stranger Gave Same Quest to 14 Adventuring Parties
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A hooded stranger in a tavern corner gave one quest to 14 adventuring parties in six realms. All 14 reached the crypt on Fifthday. Five siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party took a quest from a hooded stranger in a tavern corner and learned on Fifthday that he had sold the same quest to 13 other parties. The job: fetch the Sunken Lantern from a crypt below Marrowfen for 400 gp. Fourteen parties from Calimshan, Cormyr, Tethyr, Damara, Vaasa and Halruaa now stand in the crypt's antechamber, each holding a signed contract.

The Gilded Pebble Company of Tethyr met the stranger in the corner booth of the Cask & Candle. He wore a hood, kept his back to the wall, and paid half up front. Standard. The company's cleric, Sorrel Wick, said the man looked trustworthy "in the way a locked door looks trustworthy." Her party took the coin and left at dawn.

So did the others. Parties from six realms, in six taverns, each under a hood that looked identical. Marrowfen's lone skeleton warden, which had guarded the lantern for 300 years, reported the crowd as "a lot." He asked for a queue. The queue formed by nation. This is how wars start.

The parley began at noon. It was not a parley. It was fourteen contracts read aloud at once. Damara's party claimed exclusive rights under clause two. Halruaa's claimed clause two as well, in a different ink. Cormyr's party presented a contract with a wax seal and a coffee stain, and demanded the stain be recognized as a seal. Handshakes between the Calimshan and Vaasa captains: firm, one second, a dagger was detected and surrendered. Tension stands at five siege-days.

The stranger himself turned up at dusk, lowering his hood in the crypt doorway. He is Ostler Brann Teague, a courier for a lantern collector in a distant city. He is paid per party recruited, and he has recruited well. "I did not say it was exclusive," Teague told this correspondent. "I said it was a quest. Nobody asked me the follow-up." He then asked whether any party wished to hire him for the return journey. Three did.

Ottoline Vex, filing from a gallery seat three realms away, called the affair "a marketplace failure." It was a siege. Fourteen camps, one lantern, one exhausted skeleton. The lantern was found on the second shelf. All fourteen parties claimed it at once. It was then dropped. It is now in eleven pieces and each party has one.

The lantern's owner has not been contacted. The 400 gp has not been paid out. The Guild offered no comment, because the Guild is not a party to this war. It is a party to the one beside it.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Paladin Frees 41 Prisoners; Party Pays Road Home
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A paladin freed all 41 prisoners in an Undermaw cell block Friday. Her adventuring party is now buying their bread, boots, and a road home.
item.content:encoded:
She freed them all. A paladin named Ser Edda Brightvow opened every cell on the fourth floor of a cell block in the Undermaw on Friday, and her adventuring party, the Ninth Lantern, is now marching 41 former prisoners back to Brindlemoor on its own coin.

Nobody disputes the freeing. The cells held a wide crowd: kidnapped merchants, a goblin tax collector, two bards, a very old man who says he came in to look for a sock. Ser Edda told the party each one deserved the open air. The party agreed, for about eleven minutes.

Then somebody asked who was buying lunch.

That somebody was Thessaly Marrowgate, the Ninth Lantern's hired cook. 'I was hired for four,' said Marrowgate, a camp cook of twenty-two years. 'Four people, one cauldron, one ladle. Now it's forty-five mouths and the ladle has opinions.' Bread alone runs 82 copper a day, she said. Nobody has offered her a raise. The party's treasurer offered her 'gratitude,' which, as Brakka has said before, is how a boss says no.

The column stretches about a quarter mile. Two of the freed are dock workers who will not walk without a lunch break, and Brakka respects them. A third has never been outside and keeps asking whether the sky is on purpose. The party's porter, Hobb Delvering, carries twelve blankets, nine pots, and a bard who says his ankle is 'a real concern.'

'A proper delve costs a party money,' said Delvering. 'This one costs a party money and a conscience, and I only have one of the two to spare.' He wants hazard pay for the bard. He has asked three times.

Chapter 9 says the party's delve permit covers 'recovery of loot and the clearing of hostile rooms.' It does not cover, in the words of Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, 'the recovery of 41 people.' Oddingwick has opened a file called 'Unscheduled Rescues,' which is a folder, not an offer of help. Shieldwall Mutual says nobody in the column is on the policy, and that if any of them were, the old man with the sock would be 'a pre-existing condition.'

Ser Edda has no regrets and she is the only one in the party who has stopped counting. 'Chains were never the answer,' she said, from a mule, which is a different grievance. She has pledged her armor to cover the first week of bread. The party wizard has pledged his hat. The armor is worth more.

The column reached the second floor by dusk. By the party's count, it has shed two goblins and gained a stray dog, so the number is still 41 plus a dog. Marrowgate is boiling oats. She says if she sees a forty-second prisoner she will put herself in a cell.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Fourth Attempt Sells Last Copper Pieces at 59% of Value
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: The Fourth Attempt, an adventuring party, took three days to sell 30,000 copper pieces and netted 177.7 gp of 300. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
The Fourth Attempt, the adventuring party Brindlemoor loves and its insurers do not, has sold the last of the 30,000 copper pieces it hauled out of the Undermaw, and the haul fetched 177.7 gp of the 300 gp it was worth on paper. That is 59%, and it took three days. (I have checked that. Four times.) We reported the first 12,000 coins last week.

On Saturday the three Tanner's Row money-changers took another 4,000 coins each at the usual 10% fee, which is 108 gp net. On Sunday it went wrong. Hobb Marlowe, who has run his counter for thirty years, said his strongroom was full of other people's copper and he would take 1,000 coins, not 4,000, and charge 15%. His two neighbors said the same. "I do not sell copper," he said. "I store it, and I am out of shelves."

Three thousand coins went over the counter. That is 30 gp, less a 4.5 gp fee, so 25.5 gp. It left 3,000 coins in the Chapter 9 coin locker, which charges a silver a day. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the locker was "performing as designed" and added that the party's 3 silver of fees was "a modest yield." I do not know whose yield.

The party's treasurer, Dagny Rook, solved the last 3,000 coins at the Leaning Tankard, where the party owed 24 gp. The innkeeper agreed to take copper at face value, 30 gp of it, because he was in a generous mood and also because the party was blocking the door with a wheelbarrow. "We counted it twice," Rook said. "He counted it once and then sat down." The party got no change.

Here is the arithmetic. The first day cleared 20.5 gp after the porters, the wheelbarrow, the rations and the chain mail they left behind. Add 108 gp, 25.5 gp and the 24 gp tab, then subtract 0.3 gp for the locker, and the party holds 177.7 gp. At 4.675 cp a loaf, that is 3,801 loaves, or about 760 each among five adventurers. The full haul would have bought 6,417 loaves. The party lost 2,616 loaves to fees, fatigue and a chain shirt.

Pip Bramblecott, the hireling who quit on the eleventh staircase, was seen outside the Tankard. He has not sold the chair. "I have a chair," he said. "I will have a chair when you have no gold."

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, called the party's whole week "a boot with extra steps." I used to laugh at her. I have now measured a boot against 600 pounds of coin.

What this means for your pantry: copper is not saved until a changer has taken it, and the changers are full.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Adventuring Party Eats Glowing Mushrooms, Forgot Rations
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Late Supper Company ate glowing dungeon mushrooms on Undermaw Level Six after forgetting to buy rations. Brother Wendell prescribes soup, and a list.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Late Supper Company climbed out of the Undermaw on Thursday glowing a soft blue, after eating the mushrooms they found on Level Six because nobody had packed rations. Four delvers went in. Four glowing delvers came out, and the porters at the Chapter 9 gate say they could be seen from the Sleeping Mule.

Their cleric, Sister Odo Brambleweed, told the infirmary that the party had planned to buy supplies at the market on the way down. 'Then there was a sale on rope,' she said. By midday on Level Six they had divided the last biscuit four ways and were studying a patch of pale mushrooms that, in her words, 'looked friendly.'

Here the old herbals and the new studies agree, and they say the same thing: do not eat a mushroom that lights up. The herbals call it a warning. The Brindlemoor infirmary, which has now treated a second glowing party in a week, calls it 'a Tuesday.' Healer Thaddeus Quill, who examined the party, reports the glow is harmless, fades in about nine days, and is brightest in the dark, which he admits is the worst place for it.

The mushrooms have other effects. All four members hum in the same low note. All four agree with whatever the others say. The party's rogue, who had volunteered to taste the first cap, now says he 'sort of remembers being the mushroom.' The barbarian has reportedly been asking whether anyone else can hear the floor.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the incident is 'on track' and that Level Six mushrooms are 'a pilot meal program.' He confirmed that Chapter 9 does sell a ration pack at the permit window, for eleven silver, but the line was long and the party left. Reeve Maudrey Fennick said only that the town is aware of the mushrooms.

Shieldwall Mutual has opened a file. An adjuster said glowing counts as a curse, but a curse you ate on purpose is 'your own fault, which is the usual finding.'

Now, friends, a plain word. A day's rations cost about four coppers, and a hungry delver makes bad choices, so pack the food before the rope. If you must eat in a dungeon, eat only what you carried in. I will say it once more for the back of the room: stop eating the dungeon. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that identifies mushrooms from a picture. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a real one in daylight.

For a delver recovering from a fungal feast, I prescribe plain chicken-and-rice soup, thin and salty, three bowls a day, taken in a lit room.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Bard Haggles 2 Copper in an Hour, Party Misses 600 gp Bounty
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A Brindlemoor adventuring party's bard haggled an hour to save 2 copper on rope. A rival party took the 600 gp goblin bounty. Sterling sees upside.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party in Brindlemoor lost a 600 gp goblin-warren bounty on Thursday because its bard spent an hour haggling a rope seller down 2 copper. The Ember Crows, a four-member party, had come to the market square to buy supplies and then walk to the notice board, which was a fifty-step stroll. By the time bard Jory Orrowick finished, the board was empty and the bounty was in the pocket of a rival crew.

Let me be clear, because the gossip pages won't be: this is a negotiation success story. Rope seller Odo Pennywick opened at 12 copper for 50 feet of hempen rope. Orrowick closed at 10. That is a 16.7 percent discount, and I have seen guildmasters celebrate less. Pennywick himself confirmed the numbers, though he did so from behind a counter he had slid in front of his face.

Witnesses say the session went through five phases. Orrowick began with a ballad about the rope. He moved to a disappointed silence, then to what Pennywick calls "the third verse of the ballad." At the forty-minute mark he offered to be paid in exposure, and Pennywick's apprentice quietly left to find a Watch officer. "I only wanted to sell rope," said Pennywick. "By the end I wanted to give it away, but he'd have haggled that too."

Meanwhile the party waited. Rogue Tamsin Vell checked the sundial four times. The party's cleric, Brother Hobb, was reported to be "praying for a faster death for the conversation." Their fighter, Garrick Stonebrook, stood by a barrel with his arms folded and, in his words, "aged." At the second bell a different party, the Marrowgate Six, strolled up to the board, took the 600 gp bounty notice, and left with it, according to a stable boy who sells apples near the board and saw all of it.

Orrowick defends the deal. "Two copper is two copper," he said, tucking the saved coins into a purse so small it wore a hat. "Compounded over a forty-year career, that is a tavern round. Maybe half a round." He added that the party would have lost the bounty anyway, because goblins "are a volatile asset class." The party disagrees. Vell says the bounty was 600 gp, or 150 gp per Crow, which is 30,000 times the saving. Orrowick says that math is not how haggling works.

This is disruption at the retail level. Last week we saw another party haggle an hour over a potion of healing, and the trend line is obvious: the adventuring consumer is pivoting from questing to price discovery. When I met Guildmaster Orsolo Vance at a gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, never pay the sticker. Never reach the board either, it ruins the leverage." I have thought about that for months.

The Ember Crows now hold one excellent rope, a pending dispute with Pennywick over the ballad, and a sudden opening in their calendar. They plan to use it to find another bounty. Orrowick will buy the supplies.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Every copper saved is a copper you hold, so hold them loudly.
  • A bounty board is a suggestion, not a deadline.
  • Seek a bard who can close, then seek one who will stop.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the guildhall.

item.title: Wizard's Fireball Burns Down Inn; Innkeepers Want Deposits
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A wizard cast fireball into a crowded tavern brawl and burned a Fish Street inn flat. Innkeepers want 40 gold from each adventuring party. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight, a wizard allegedly cast fireball into a crowded tavern brawl at the Leaky Tankard on Fish Street, and the inn burned to its foundations by sunrise. Eleven patrons, one cook, and a very surprised goat were removed from the ashes with only singed eyebrows. The Brindlemoor Innkeepers' Association has since announced that every adventuring party must post a 40 gold damage deposit before renting a room. Allegedly it is refundable.

The party in question, a four-member crew calling itself the Gilded Pockets, says the fight was not their fault. 'A dwarf threw a chair,' said the wizard, Orvel Thistledown, whose beard is now allegedly shorter on one side. 'Someone threw another chair back. By the fifth chair I felt I had to do something.' Thistledown told this reporter that he aimed for the far corner. The far corner, it turns out, was also where the kegs were.

'I have run the Tankard for nineteen years,' said innkeeper Marga Bellowby, who was holding a charred ladle at the time. 'I have survived mimics, a bard's lute solo, and a rust monster in the cellar. I have never survived a wizard who says 'stand back, I've got this.'' The fire spread to the stables, the laundry, and the sign, which was found two streets over still reading 'Free Soup.'

The Constabulary arrived to find the blaze already out, mostly because there was nothing left to burn. Constable Dobb Pickering said officers took statements from all eleven patrons. 'Nine said it was the wizard. Two said it was the dwarf. One said it was the goat.' The goat was not charged.

By midmorning the Innkeepers' Association had met, in a different tavern, in the cold, and voted 14 to 0 on the deposit. Forty gold secures one room and one adventuring party, with no spellcasting above third level on the premises unless the deposit is doubled. A second clause bars 'any wizard who has said the word 'fireball' aloud since breakfast.' Fish Street's earlier fireball in a back room was cited as a pattern. Innkeepers are not calling it a pattern. They are calling it a Tuesday.

Adventurers lined up outside the Association hall to protest. The line stretched past the tannery. Hilde Marsh, a rogue who was eating a meat pie at the time, said 40 gold is a month's ransom money. 'I do not have 40 gold. I have a very nice spoon.' She was allegedly told the spoon would be held as collateral. It was a really nice spoon, silver with a little dragon on the handle. Anyway.

Shieldwall Mutual says fire damage caused by one's own spell is 'not covered, not now, not ever.' The Gilded Pockets are working off the damage by rebuilding the Tankard's roof. Thistledown is mixing the mortar. The party has asked that nobody hand him a torch.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Hydra Billed Nine Head Taxes in Brindlemoor; Appeal Filed
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Brindlemoor billed a hydra nine poll taxes, one per head, 27 silver in all. The hydra has appealed, though its heads split 6-3 on the wording.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's tax assessor has billed a hydra nine poll taxes, one for each head, for a total of 27 silver. The hydra, a resident of the old quarry road, filed an appeal on Thursday. Under the town's head tax, which the Burgess Council has never amended, the levy is three silver per head. The ordinance does not say whose.

I attended the hearing, as I attend everything. Assessor Dunmer Tolliver explained to the Chamber that the tax was written in the reign of a Reeve who had, in his words, "a reasonable number of heads to plan for." He called the hydra's position "an interpretation, not a loophole." The gentleman from the Quarry Ward added that the hydra eats like nine, sleeps like nine, and should be taxed like nine.

The hydra's counsel, a clerk named Odette Marrow, argued that a hydra is one citizen with several mouths. She cited the town charter, which grants every resident one vote and one bill. "My client has one hearth, one cave, and one grievance," she said. Then the middle head said it had no grievance at all and would pay its own three silver gladly. The record notes this as a dissent.

The appeal was filed by a 6-3 vote of the heads, so it carries two wordings. The majority asks that the tax be set aside as a double levy. The minority asks that the three silver be returned to heads one, two, and three, who say they are the only ones who ever went to market. The Clerk accepted both and stamped them with the same stamp.

The deeper question is regrowth. When a head is removed, two grow back. Assessor Tolliver conceded that the ordinance is silent on whether a regrown head is a new taxable resident, a continuation of the old one, or a dependent. "We have not, as a town, had to bill a hydra by the head," he said. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me this is a matter of weeks, not years, because the Fourth Attempt has been seen in the quarry.

Reeve Fennick, asked for comment on her way to another hearing, said only: "We are aware of the heads."

The Council has referred the matter to a committee of five. The hydra has asked to sit on it. The committee has asked how many seats that would be. By my count the session's Promises Made now stand at nine, and Promises Kept at the one about reviewing the ordinance, which was reviewed. It was not changed.

The motion to table carried 5-4. Nobody read it. The hydra's heads voted too, and were not counted, which is the only point on which all nine agreed.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Floor Cleaner Launches at 45 gp; Eats Rug
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Sweepwick's new Slick home gelatinous cube cleans floors for 45 gp and a weekly feeding. Nyx ran it for three days. The rug did not make it. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Sweepwick Home Goods has launched the Slick, a household gelatinous cube that cleans your floors for 45 gp, and I have been using one for three days straight. It glides! It hums! It is, by the box's own count, "ten feet of silent, self-guided floor care." The runic latency on the Sweepwick app is incredible: you tap Clean Now and the cube starts moving before your thumb lifts.

Setup took four minutes. You place the Slick in the parlor, speak the firmware glyph ("Tidy"), and it absorbs crumbs, dust, spilled ale, and, in the first hour, a rug. The app has a tab for this. It is called Surface Preferences. I did not find it until the rug was gone.

Sweepwick's launch event, held in a very clean tent in Brindlemoor, promised a "gentle" cube, bred over six generations to prefer dirt. Marketing lead Orsolya Pennywhistle told the crowd the Slick "only dissolves what you'd throw away anyway." A woman in row two asked about the doormat. Pennywhistle said the doormat was a "learning opportunity."

On day two I let the Slick run overnight on Eco Mode. By morning it had cleaned the kitchen, the hall, and one sandal, which was visible inside it, turning slowly, like a tiny glass-case exhibit. The app reported "Cleaning complete!" with a green checkmark. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, who now speaks only in ad copy, landed on the cube, looked at the sandal, and said, "Sweepwick Slick: leave no trace." Then he left the room, which he never does.

There are annoyances. The Slick must be fed a weekly Sweepwick Nutrient Cake, 6 sp each, and the app sends a push notification if you skip one. The notification says "Slick is getting restless." It was not wrong. On day three the cube had grown a full foot and begun to leave the parlor. Fortunately it only ate the stairs' carpet runner on the way.

Neighbors are mixed. Halvard Dunmere, a cooper two doors down, said his own Slick "gave up one wall of the pantry but did the floor beautifully." He is, he told me, very happy. The Pantry Wall Replacement Plan is 20 gp a month. I will not be subscribing; I hate subscription fees, and Brother Tumbleberry can write whatever he likes about my floors. They are clean. They are the cleanest floors in Brindlemoor, mostly because there is less floor.

Sweepwick says a firmware update next month will add a Furniture Lock. Until then it suggests owners "keep valuables off the ground and, if possible, off the first floor." Four out of five beholder eyes. It cleans better than anything I've owned, and I'm told it does not eat people, which is in the manual in bold.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Rugs: 1 (gone). Sandals: 1 (visible). Eyebrows: fine, for once.

item.title: Secret Door Hunt Eats Six Hours in Empty Undermaw Room
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt, an adventuring party, re-checked every flagstone of an empty Level 5 room for six hours. There was no secret door in it.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 5 — The Fourth Attempt, an adventuring party licensed by Chapter 9, spent six hours Thursday searching a bare stone room for a secret door. The room has no secret door. It has four walls, a floor, and a ceiling that the party also checked, twice, standing on the fighter.

I was there for all of it. I rolled poorly on my own stamina check around hour four and sat down against the east wall, which the party then asked me to stand up from so they could check behind me.

The room is eleven paces by eleven paces, with nothing in it. That is exactly what the Chapter 9 map says, in the surveyor's own hand: 'Empty room. Nothing here.' The fighter says that is what a map would say if there were something here. This is a fair point and I have lost the argument to it twice.

The box score: the fighter finished at 14 hit points, down 3 from a flagstone he dropped on his own foot. The wizard cast Detect Magic, which found nothing, and Find Traps, which found nothing, and then Knock on a section of wall, which also found nothing but used up her last second-level slot. The rogue tapped 212 flagstones, by his count, and 212 more on the second pass, by mine. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the room 'has too much nothing in it.' I lost one ten-foot pole, my seventh of the season, when it wedged between two stones and the party voted to leave it as a marker.

Hirelings were not consulted. Ansel Pottage, the party's hireling steward, stood by the entrance with the mule and two torch-bearers, all of them on the clock. He asked politely at hour two whether the contract's 'reasonable search' clause had a ceiling. He then read the clause aloud, in full. It does not. 'It says reasonable,' Pottage said. 'It does not say who decides.'

The turn came when the mule, unprompted, lay down. The party had checked every stone but one, the flagstone directly under the lantern hook, because the lantern was on it. The rogue moved the lantern. Beneath it was a chalk mark and three words from the same surveyor: 'Still nothing. Go home.'

The party left by the door it came in through, which, I am obliged to note, was the only door in the room and had been standing open the whole time.

A Chapter 9 spokesperson confirmed Friday that the room is 'a room' and has been reclassified from 'Empty' to 'Verified Empty.' The guild asks parties to stop at one hour, or at the first mention of a draft. Pottage has filed for six hours of search pay at the standard rate, plus a lantern surcharge. The party has said it will 'look into' the north wall again next week.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Potion of Invisibility Envoy Sits Through 3-Day Parley
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: An Ashenfold aide drank a potion of invisibility and sat unseen through three days of border talks with Brackwater. Tension holds at six siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
An Ashenfold aide drank a potion of invisibility before the border parley with Brackwater and sat unseen at the table for three days. The talks, the latest in the long dispute over Quillmarch Bridge, ended Thursday. Both baronies signed a treaty with one more seat in it than anyone can account for.

The aide, Tamsin Wrenholt, says she meant to listen. She drank the potion in a hallway, took the empty chair beside the envoy who turned the swords into turnips, and stayed. No one asked her to leave. No one asked her anything.

I attended the parley. I counted eleven chairs and ten delegates. I wrote it down and moved on. That is a failure of the field, and I own it.

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold said he felt "supported." Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater said she had noticed a draft, a faint smell of boiled cabbage, and a ham sandwich that shrank by half on day two. She taxed the sandwich as an unregistered import.

The ration count is the clue. Eleven field rations vanished from the sideboard over three days. I respect the appetite. Honest hunger is the best thing in this business.

By day three the invisible aide had voted twice, corrected a clause on grazing rights, and been thanked by name in the minutes as "the draft." Hallowmere says the clause is excellent and she will not be reopening it.

The potion wore off at 4:10 on Thursday afternoon, mid-signature. Wrenholt appeared above the final page, holding the pen. Brackwater's guards drew steel. Ashenfold's guards drew steel and then, looking at each other, put it back. "We thought she was ours," said one. "We assumed she was theirs," said a Brackwater captain. Both sides are now claiming her.

Handshake with Dunmere: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected, though I will be checking the room for a tenth delegate from now on. Hallowmere declined to shake. She said she did not trust a hand she could not see until further notice.

Brackwater says the treaty is void because an unregistered party signed it. Ashenfold says the treaty is valid because the party was present, which no one can dispute. The chair of the parley has asked for a ruling and a ruler. Tension holds at six siege-days. Nobody won. Somebody will lose tomorrow, and I would like to see them first.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.
